claim: Stress fibers (SFs) are actomyosin bundles commonly found in individually migrating cells in culture.
source: Stress fibers (SFs) are actomyosin bundles commonly found in individually migrating cells in culture.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about stress fibers in the field.

claim: SFs have been categorized into different types based on their origin, subcellular location, and how they interact with nonmuscle myosin II and integrin-based focal adhesions.
source: SFs are prominent F-actin bundles that have been categorized into different types based on their origin, subcellular location, and how they interact with nonmuscle myosin II and integrin-based focal adhesions (Burridge and Guilluy, 2016; Burridge and Wittchen, 2013; Naumanen et al., 2008; Tojkander et al., 2012; Vallenius, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The most studied SF types have myosin along their lengths and large focal adhesions at either end.
source: The most studied SF types have myosin along their lengths and large focal adhesions at either end; these include ventral SFs (Hotulainen and Lappalainen, 2006; Tojkander et al., 2015) and the recently defined cortical SFs (Lehtimäki et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SFs play key roles in focal adhesion maturation, defining the cell's front–rear axis, retraction of the trailing edge, and sensing the mechanical properties of the ECM.
source: SFs play key roles in focal adhesion maturation, defining the cell's front–rear axis, retraction of the trailing edge, and sensing the mechanical properties of the ECM (Lehtimäki et al., 2017; Livne and Geiger, 2016; Schwartz, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Current knowledge of SFs in migrating cells comes almost entirely from studies of individual cells on nonnative substrates.
source: However, our current knowledge of SFs in migrating cells comes almost entirely from studies of individual cells on nonnative substrates.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Whether and how cells use SFs to migrate in vivo or as part of a collective is largely unknown.
source: Whether and how cells use SFs to migrate in vivo or as part of a collective is largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: An egg chamber is an ovarian follicle that will give rise to one egg.
source: An egg chamber is an ovarian follicle that will give rise to one egg.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila egg chamber biology.

claim: The egg chamber has a central cluster of germ cells surrounded by a somatic follicular epithelium.
source: It has a central cluster of germ cells surrounded by a somatic follicular epithelium; a basement membrane ECM encapsulates the entire structure (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by description in text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A basement membrane ECM encapsulates the entire egg chamber structure.
source: It has a central cluster of germ cells surrounded by a somatic follicular epithelium; a basement membrane ECM encapsulates the entire structure (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by description in text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: During early stages of oogenesis, the basal surfaces of the follicle cells collectively migrate along the basement membrane.
source: During early stages of oogenesis, the basal surfaces of the follicle cells collectively migrate along the basement membrane (Cetera et al., 2014; Lewellyn et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Collective migration of follicle cells causes the entire egg chamber to rotate within the basement membrane.
source: This causes the entire egg chamber to rotate within the basement membrane, which itself remains stationary (Haigo and Bilder, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The basement membrane remains stationary during egg chamber rotation.
source: This causes the entire egg chamber to rotate within the basement membrane, which itself remains stationary (Haigo and Bilder, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: During migration, each follicle cell has actin-based protrusions at its leading edge.
source: During this migration, each follicle cell has actin-based protrusions at its leading edge and a parallel array of SFs across its basal surface that are oriented in the direction of tissue movement (Cetera et al., 2014; Gutzeit, 1991; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: During migration, each follicle cell has a parallel array of SFs across its basal surface that are oriented in the direction of tissue movement.
source: During this migration, each follicle cell has actin-based protrusions at its leading edge and a parallel array of SFs across its basal surface that are oriented in the direction of tissue movement (Cetera et al., 2014; Gutzeit, 1991; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At later stages when the follicle cells have stopped migrating, the density of SFs across the basal surface increases.
source: At later stages when the follicle cells have stopped migrating, the density of SFs across the basal surface increases (Delon and Brown, 2009; Gutzeit, 1991; Gutzeit, 1990), and their contractile activity helps to create the elongated shape of the egg (Cerqueira Campos et al., 2020; He et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The contractile activity of SFs helps to create the elongated shape of the egg.
source: At later stages when the follicle cells have stopped migrating, the density of SFs across the basal surface increases (Delon and Brown, 2009; Gutzeit, 1991; Gutzeit, 1990), and their contractile activity helps to create the elongated shape of the egg (Cerqueira Campos et al., 2020; He et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The SFs in the follicle cells have many internal adhesions along their lengths, in addition to adhesions at the ends.
source: Here, we show that the SFs in the follicle cells have many internal adhesions along their lengths, in addition to adhesions at the ends.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: SFs in follicle cells undergo a novel treadmilling behavior that allows them to persist as the cell migrates over more than one cell length.
source: We further show that these SFs undergo a novel treadmilling behavior that allows them to persist as the cell migrates over more than one cell length.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Treadmilling SFs grow at their fronts by adding new adhesions and actomyosin segments over time.
source: Treadmilling SFs grow at their fronts by adding new adhesions and actomyosin segments over time.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Front-forming adhesions remain stationary relative to the substrate.
source: The front-forming adhesions remain stationary relative to the substrate and typically disassemble as the cell rear approaches.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Front-forming adhesions typically disassemble as the cell rear approaches.
source: The front-forming adhesions remain stationary relative to the substrate and typically disassemble as the cell rear approaches.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: A different type of adhesion forms at the SF's terminus that slides with the cell's trailing edge as the actomyosin ahead of it shortens.
source: By contrast, a different type of adhesion forms at the SF's terminus that slides with the cell's trailing edge as the actomyosin ahead of it shortens.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: SF treadmilling depends on cell movement.
source: We further show that SF treadmilling depends on cell movement and identify a developmental switch in the formins that mediate SF assembly, with Dishevelled-associated activator of morphogenesis acting during migratory stages and Diaphanous acting during postmigratory stages.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: There is a developmental switch in the formins that mediate SF assembly, with DAAM acting during migratory stages and Diaphanous acting during postmigratory stages.
source: We further show that SF treadmilling depends on cell movement and identify a developmental switch in the formins that mediate SF assembly, with Dishevelled-associated activator of morphogenesis acting during migratory stages and Diaphanous acting during postmigratory stages.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: Treadmilling SFs keep each cell on a linear trajectory, thereby promoting the collective motility required for epithelial migration.
source: We propose that treadmilling SFs keep each cell on a linear trajectory, thereby promoting the collective motility required for epithelial migration.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: MRLC-GFP labels SFs but not leading-edge protrusions.
source: Image of one cell showing that myosin regulatory light chain (MRLC-GFP) labels SFs, but not leading-edge protrusions. Image shown is representative of five egg chambers.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A with representative data from five egg chambers.

claim: New SFs appear by rapid coalescence of MRLC.
source: Appearance of a new SF is marked by a rapid coalescence of MRLC (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B with quantification of 64 SF appearances.

claim: SFs disappear either by fading along their lengths or by contracting rapidly from the rear.
source: SFs disappear either by fading along their lengths or by contracting rapidly from the rear (Figure 2C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2C with quantification of 75 SF disappearances.

claim: SFs have a half-life of 34 minutes.
source: Through this assay, we determined that these SFs have a half-life of 34 min.
evidence: Measured from data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only 60% of SFs both appeared and disappeared during the 60-min imaging window.
source: This is clearly an underestimate, however, as only 60% of SFs both appeared and disappeared during the 60-min window.
evidence: Based on analysis of SF lifetimes from video data.

claim: For 32% of SFs, either their appearance or disappearance but not both was observed during the 60-min window.
source: For 32% of SFs, we saw either their appearance or disappearance but not both.
evidence: Based on analysis of SF lifetimes from video data.

claim: 8% of SFs persisted for the entire 60 minutes of imaging.
source: The remaining 8% persisted for the entire 60 min.
evidence: Based on analysis of SF lifetimes from video data.

claim: Follicle cells migrated a mean distance of 16.8 µm during the 60-minute assay, corresponding to a mean of 2.2 cell lengths.
source: The follicle cells migrated a mean distance of 16.8 µm in this assay, corresponding to a mean of 2.2 cell lengths.
evidence: Measured from video data, n = 91 SFs from 23 cells in 3 egg chambers.

claim: 62% of SFs persisted for longer than the time required for the cell to travel at least one cell length.
source: Strikingly, 62% of SFs persisted for longer than the time required for the cell to travel at least one cell length (Figure 2E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2E, n = 91 SFs from 23 cells in 3 egg chambers.

claim: New actomyosin segments are added to the front of existing SFs.
source: Indeed, new actomyosin segments are added to the front of existing SFs (Figure 2F–H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C, and Figure 2—video 2), which explains their persistence.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2F-H and supplementary figures.

claim: At postmigratory stages, SFs exhibit the canonical organization with large focal adhesions at their ends.
source: Previous descriptions of these adhesions in follicle cells primarily focused on later stages of egg chamber development (Delon and Brown, 2009), after the follicle cells have ceased migrating. At these later stages, the SFs are increased in density across the basal surface, and they exhibit the canonical organization with large focal adhesions at their ends (Figure 3A–D, G).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A-D, G with citation to prior work.

claim: The SFs present during migratory stages have many smaller adhesions along their lengths.
source: By contrast, the SFs present during migratory stages have many smaller adhesions along their lengths (Figure 3A, G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Cetera et al., 2014), with an average of 5.5 adhesions per fiber.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A, G and supplementary figure, with citation to prior work.

claim: SFs during migratory stages have an average of 5.5 adhesions per fiber.
source: By contrast, the SFs present during migratory stages have many smaller adhesions along their lengths (Figure 3A, G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Cetera et al., 2014), with an average of 5.5 adhesions per fiber.
evidence: Quantified from data shown in Figure 3E, F.

claim: Multiple adhesions along SF lengths are visible with endogenous GFP tags on Paxillin, Talin, and the βPS-integrin subunit Myospheroid.
source: This phenomenon is easiest to see when Paxillin-GFP is overexpressed (UAS-Pax-GFP) (Figure 3A); however, we also see multiple adhesions with endogenous GFP tags on Paxillin, Talin, and the βPS-integrin subunit, Myospheroid (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3B-D with endogenous tags.

claim: New adhesions and new segments of actomyosin are continuously added to the front of a SF over time.
source: This analysis showed that new adhesions and new segments of actomyosin are continuously added to the front of a SF over time (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown in kymograph analysis in Figure 4A, representative of 8 SFs.

claim: A front-forming adhesion typically first appears near the cell's leading edge and grows in brightness as an actomyosin segment coalesces behind it.
source: A front-forming adhesion typically first appears near the cell's leading edge and grows in brightness as an actomyosin segment coalesces behind it to link the new adhesion to an existing SF (Figure 4C).
evidence: Shown in kymograph analysis in Figure 4C, representative of 7 SFs.

claim: New adhesions are pulled slightly rearward, consistent with their maturing under tension.
source: New adhesions are also pulled slightly rearward, consistent with their maturing under tension.
evidence: Observed in kymograph analysis and interpreted based on known adhesion behavior.

claim: For 82% of the SFs analyzed, the final adhesion at the SF terminus appears to slide along the substrate at the same speed that the cell migrates.
source: We noted that a different type of adhesion forms at the back of the cell. For 82% of the SFs analyzed, the final adhesion at the SF terminus appears to slide along the substrate at the same speed that the cell migrates (Figure 4A, D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A, D with quantification from 23 cells in 3 egg chambers.

claim: 80% of sliding adhesions arise de novo near the cell's trailing edge.
source: Sliding adhesions can arise from stationary adhesions; however, 80% arise de novo near the cell's trailing edge.
evidence: Quantified from video analysis of adhesion dynamics.

claim: Sliding adhesions persist for a mean of 34 minutes, which corresponds to the time required for a cell to migrate 1.2 cell lengths.
source: Sliding adhesions are remarkably long lived, persisting for a mean of 34 min, which corresponds to the time required for a cell to migrate 1.2 cell lengths.
evidence: Quantified from data shown in Figure 4E, n = 84 adhesions from 23 cells in 3 egg chambers.

claim: Stationary adhesions persist for only a mean of 13 minutes.
source: By contrast, stationary adhesions persist for only a mean of 13 min (Figure 4E).
evidence: Quantified from data shown in Figure 4E, n = 134 adhesions from 23 cells in 3 egg chambers.

claim: Stationary adhesions typically disassemble before they reach the cell's trailing edge.
source: Stationary adhesions typically disassemble before they reach the cell's trailing edge.
evidence: Observed from video analysis of adhesion dynamics.

claim: ~20% of stationary adhesions are subsumed by sliding adhesions.
source: However, ~20% of stationary adhesions are subsumed by sliding adhesions (Figure 4D and Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4D and video, quantified from adhesion dynamics analysis.

claim: 74% of sliding adhesions merged with at least one stationary adhesion.
source: We observed that 74% of sliding adhesions merged with at least one stationary adhesion, which may account for their long lifetimes.
evidence: Quantified from video analysis of adhesion dynamics.

claim: Inhibition of Arp2/3 by CK-666 eliminates leading-edge F-actin networks in follicle cells.
source: We blocked follicle cell migration by employing two methods that eliminate leading-edge F-actin networks in these cells, inhibition of Arp2/3 by CK-666, and depletion of the Scar/WAVE complex with RNAi against Abelson interacting protein (Abi RNAi).
evidence: Experimental manipulation described with results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Depletion of the Scar/WAVE complex with Abi RNAi eliminates leading-edge F-actin networks in follicle cells.
source: We blocked follicle cell migration by employing two methods that eliminate leading-edge F-actin networks in these cells, inhibition of Arp2/3 by CK-666, and depletion of the Scar/WAVE complex with RNAi against Abelson interacting protein (Abi RNAi).
evidence: Experimental manipulation described with results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both CK-666 treatment and Abi RNAi cause SFs to adopt a canonical architecture, in which the adhesions become concentrated at the ends.
source: Analysis of fixed samples revealed that both treatments cause SFs to adopt a canonical architecture, in which the adhesions become concentrated at the ends (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A, n = 28 (DMSO), n = 29 (CK-666), and n = 16 (Abi RNAi) egg chambers.

claim: Following addition of CK-666, internal adhesions disappear over time as the end adhesions grow and myosin becomes concentrated in the center.
source: Following addition of CK-666, the follicle cells gradually come to a stop. The internal adhesions disappear over time as the end adhesions grow and myosin becomes concentrated in the center (Figure 5B and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5B and video, representative of 8 egg chambers.

claim: Once the transition to canonical SF architecture is complete, individual SFs often contract from both ends toward the center and disappear.
source: Once this transition is complete, individual SFs often contract from both ends toward the center and disappear; new adhesions are never added to their ends (Figure 5C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5C, representative of most SFs in 8 egg chambers.

claim: New adhesions are never added to the ends of SFs after migration is blocked.
source: Once this transition is complete, individual SFs often contract from both ends toward the center and disappear; new adhesions are never added to their ends (Figure 5C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5C, representative of most SFs in 8 egg chambers.

claim: SFs within RNAi-expressing clones in mosaic epithelia show the same modular architecture and treadmilling behavior as wild-type SFs.
source: Importantly, the SFs within the RNAi-expressing clones show the same modular architecture and treadmilling behavior as wild-type SFs (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5D, E, representative of 6 and 3 egg chambers respectively.

claim: It is migration itself, not the activity of the Scar/WAVE complex, that is necessary to generate treadmilling SFs.
source: We therefore conclude that it is migration itself, not the activity of the Scar/WAVE complex, that is necessary to generate treadmilling SFs.
evidence: Conclusion based on comparison of mosaic and tissue-wide Scar/WAVE depletion experiments.

claim: Elimination of leading-edge F-actin networks through depletion of the Scar/WAVE complex did not reduce F-actin levels in the SFs.
source: However, elimination of leading-edge F-actin networks through depletion of the Scar/WAVE complex did not reduce F-actin levels in the SFs (Figure 6A, D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6A, D and supplementary figure, n = 7 egg chambers.

claim: Depletion of Enabled, which builds leading-edge filopodia, does not reduce F-actin levels in SFs.
source: This is also true for cells depleted of Enabled, which builds leading-edge filopodia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C; Cetera et al., 2014).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C with citation.

claim: The leading edge is not a major source of F-actin for SFs in follicle cells.
source: Hence, the leading edge is not a major source of F-actin for these SFs.
evidence: Conclusion based on experiments depleting leading-edge F-actin components.

claim: Depleting DAAM reduces F-actin levels in the SFs by ~30%.
source: We performed an RNAi-based screen of Drosophila formins and found that depleting DAAM reduces F-actin levels in the SFs by ~30% (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, Figure 6B, D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6B, D and supplementary figure, n = 13 egg chambers for DAAM RNAi.

claim: Two null alleles of DAAM reduce F-actin in the SFs without having obvious effects on other F-actin populations.
source: We confirmed this result by showing that two null alleles of DAAM similarly reduce F-actin in the SFs without having obvious effects on other F-actin populations (Figure 6B, D, E), and that an activated form of DAAM increases F-actin in the SFs (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6B, D, E, n = 17 and 10 egg chambers for the two alleles.

claim: An activated form of DAAM increases F-actin in the SFs.
source: We confirmed this result by showing that two null alleles of DAAM similarly reduce F-actin in the SFs without having obvious effects on other F-actin populations (Figure 6B, D, E), and that an activated form of DAAM increases F-actin in the SFs (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6C, D, n = 10 egg chambers.

claim: RNAi against other formins had no effect on the SFs.
source: RNAi against other formins had no effect on the SFs, nor did codepleting formins or other F-actin assembly factors with DAAM (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, E with multiple formin RNAi lines tested.

claim: DAAM is a key contributor to treadmilling SF assembly.
source: From these data, we conclude that DAAM is a key contributor to treadmilling SF assembly.
evidence: Conclusion based on DAAM depletion and overexpression experiments.

claim: DAAM localizes largely uniformly within the cortex with no obvious enrichment on SFs or adhesions.
source: Using a line in which DAAM is endogenously tagged with GFP (DAAM-GFP) (Molnár et al., 2014), we found that DAAM localizes largely uniformly within the cortex with no obvious enrichment on SFs or adhesions (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7A, B, representative of 5 egg chambers, with citation.

claim: DAAM-depleted cells have the same density of SFs across their basal surfaces as control cells.
source: DAAM-depleted cells have the same density of SFs across their basal surfaces as control cells (Figure 7C, D); each one simply has reduced levels of F-actin, myosin, and the focal adhesion protein Talin (Figures 6D and 7C, E, F).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7C, D, n = 90 cells from 9 egg chambers.

claim: DAAM-depleted SFs have reduced levels of F-actin, myosin, and the focal adhesion protein Talin.
source: DAAM-depleted cells have the same density of SFs across their basal surfaces as control cells (Figure 7C, D); each one simply has reduced levels of F-actin, myosin, and the focal adhesion protein Talin (Figures 6D and 7C, E, F).
evidence: Shown in Figures 6D and 7C, E, F with quantification.

claim: Mean migration rates for DAAM-depleted epithelia are faster than for control epithelia.
source: Similarly, mean migration rates for DAAM-depleted epithelia are faster than for control epithelia (Figure 7G).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7G, n = 27 control and 23 DAAM RNAi egg chambers.

claim: DAAM contributes to the assembly of treadmilling SFs by adding new F-actin along their lengths, and/or by contributing F-actin to the basal cortex.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that DAAM contributes to the assembly of treadmilling SFs by adding new F-actin along their lengths, and/or by contributing F-actin to the basal cortex, and that this additional F-actin strengthens cell–ECM adhesion.
evidence: Interpretation of DAAM localization and depletion experiments.

claim: DAAM is downregulated after follicle cell migration has ceased.
source: We found that DAAM is downregulated after follicle cell migration has ceased (Figure 8A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8A with quantification across developmental stages.

claim: DAAM RNAi reduces F-actin in treadmilling SFs during migratory stages but not in canonical SFs during postmigratory stages.
source: This reduces F-actin in the treadmilling SFs as expected. During postmigratory stages, however, F-actin levels in the SFs are unaffected (Figure 8B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8B with quantification at different stages.

claim: DAAM selectively contributes to the formation of treadmilling SFs.
source: Thus, DAAM selectively contributes to the formation of treadmilling SFs.
evidence: Conclusion based on stage-specific effects of DAAM depletion.

claim: Dia RNAi does not affect treadmilling SFs during migratory stages.
source: However, when we depleted Dia during migratory stages as part of our RNAi screen, the treadmilling SFs were unaffected (Figure 8C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8C and supplementary figure.

claim: Dia RNAi-expressing clones contained multinucleated cells, consistent with Dia's role in cytokinesis.
source: We know Dia was depleted because the RNAi-expressing clones contained multinucleated cells, consistent with Dia's role in cytokinesis.
evidence: Observed phenotype consistent with known Dia function.

claim: Dia RNAi expressed using Cy2-Gal4 largely eliminates SFs from postmigratory cells.
source: To ask if Dia selectively mediates canonical SF assembly during postmigratory stages, we expressed Dia RNAi using Cy2-Gal4, which initiates expression after cell divisions and cell migration have both ceased. This condition largely eliminates SFs from postmigratory cells, while similarly expressing DAAM RNAi does not (Figure 8D, E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8D, E, n = 29 and 11 egg chambers for Dia RNAi lines.

claim: DAAM RNAi expressed using Cy2-Gal4 does not eliminate SFs from postmigratory cells.
source: To ask if Dia selectively mediates canonical SF assembly during postmigratory stages, we expressed Dia RNAi using Cy2-Gal4, which initiates expression after cell divisions and cell migration have both ceased. This condition largely eliminates SFs from postmigratory cells, while similarly expressing DAAM RNAi does not (Figure 8D, E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8D, E, n = 13 egg chambers for DAAM RNAi.

claim: There is a developmental switch in the formins that mediate SF assembly in the follicle cells, with DAAM contributing to treadmilling SFs during migratory stages and Dia contributing to the canonical SFs that form after migration is complete.
source: These data show that there is a developmental switch in the formins that mediate SF assembly in the follicle cells, with DAAM contributing to treadmilling SFs during migratory stages and Dia contributing to the canonical SFs that form after migration is complete.
evidence: Conclusion based on stage-specific effects of DAAM and Dia depletion.

claim: SFs in migrating follicle cells have internal adhesions along their lengths, in addition to adhesions at the ends.
source: We found that SFs in migrating follicle cells have internal adhesions along their lengths, in addition to adhesions at the ends.
evidence: Primary finding summarized in Discussion, supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The formation of internal adhesions depends on treadmilling.
source: In this way, the formation of internal adhesions depends on treadmilling.
evidence: Interpretation of how internal adhesions arise during SF treadmilling.

claim: Internal adhesions contribute to treadmilling by generating the modular SF architecture needed for older stationary adhesions to be disassembled near the cell's rear.
source: Once formed, the internal adhesions then contribute to treadmilling by generating the modular SF architecture needed for older stationary adhesions to be disassembled near the cell's rear and allow the back of the SF to shorten.
evidence: Interpretation of the functional role of internal adhesions.

claim: This is the first study to focus on the role of internal adhesions in SF dynamics.
source: To our knowledge this is the first study to focus on the role of internal adhesions in SF dynamics, but there are hints in the literature that these structures may exist in other cells.
evidence: Authors' assessment of the novelty of their findings.

claim: SFs isolated from human foreskin fibroblasts and bovine endothelial cells have small puncta of the focal adhesion protein vinculin along their lengths in addition to prominent vinculin puncta at their ends.
source: For example, SFs isolated from human foreskin fibroblasts and bovine endothelial cells have small puncta of the focal adhesion protein vinculin along their lengths in addition to prominent vinculin puncta at their ends (Katoh et al., 1998), and the cortical SFs in cultured mesenchymal cells were sometimes observed to have more than two adhesions (Lehtimäki et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited evidence from prior literature.

claim: Cortical SFs in cultured mesenchymal cells were sometimes observed to have more than two adhesions.
source: For example, SFs isolated from human foreskin fibroblasts and bovine endothelial cells have small puncta of the focal adhesion protein vinculin along their lengths in addition to prominent vinculin puncta at their ends (Katoh et al., 1998), and the cortical SFs in cultured mesenchymal cells were sometimes observed to have more than two adhesions (Lehtimäki et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited evidence from prior literature.

claim: Internal adhesions have been invoked as a possible explanation for the buckling pattern observed when SFs are rapidly compressed.
source: Internal adhesions have also been invoked as a possible explanation for the buckling pattern observed when SFs are rapidly compressed (Costa et al., 2002; Kassianidou and Kumar, 2015).
evidence: Cited evidence from prior literature.

claim: Internal adhesions likely experience more balanced pulling forces than end adhesions.
source: Because internal adhesions are attached to two aligned actomyosin segments, they likely experience more balanced pulling forces than end adhesions, which may affect their composition and/or organization.
evidence: Speculation based on the structural arrangement of internal adhesions.

claim: There is likely still higher tension on one side of internal adhesions due to forces exerted by cell movement.
source: It is also likely, however, that there is still higher tension on one side of the adhesion due to forces exerted by cell movement.
evidence: Speculation about forces on internal adhesions during migration.

claim: The new actomyosin segment captures a nearby nascent adhesion that has formed just behind the cell's leading edge.
source: We envision that the new actomyosin segment captures a nearby nascent adhesion that has formed just behind the cell's leading edge, and that this activity both links the nascent adhesion to the existing SF and induces it to mature.
evidence: Proposed model for how new SF segments form.

claim: DAAM could localize to nascent and mature adhesions, causing actin filaments to grow out from these sites.
source: One possibility is that DAAM localizes to nascent and mature adhesions, causing actin filaments to grow out from these sites, like the role ascribed to Dia in dorsal SF formation (Hotulainen and Lappalainen, 2006; Oakes et al., 2012; Tojkander et al., 2011).
evidence: Hypothetical mechanism for DAAM function, with citations to analogous Dia function.

claim: DAAM could play a more general role in contributing F-actin to the basal cortex along with other actin assembly factors.
source: Alternatively, DAAM could play a more general role in contributing F-actin to the basal cortex along with other actin assembly factors (Chugh and Paluch, 2018), with local pulses of myosin activity near the cell's leading-edge condensing the cortical F-actin meshwork to form the new actomyosin segment.
evidence: Alternative hypothetical mechanism for DAAM function, with citation.

claim: Treadmilling SFs closely resemble other SF types that arise from the cortex and/or are embedded within it.
source: Second, treadmilling SFs closely resemble other SF types that arise from the cortex and/or are embedded within it (Lehtimäki et al., 2021; Svitkina, 2020; Vignaud et al., 2020), as they lie so flat against the basal surface that we can visualize them with near-TIRF microscopy.
evidence: Comparison to other SF types with citations.

claim: Treadmilling SFs lie so flat against the basal surface that they can be visualized with near-TIRF microscopy.
source: Second, treadmilling SFs closely resemble other SF types that arise from the cortex and/or are embedded within it (Lehtimäki et al., 2021; Svitkina, 2020; Vignaud et al., 2020), as they lie so flat against the basal surface that we can visualize them with near-TIRF microscopy.
evidence: Observation from imaging experiments.

claim: Ventral SFs have centers that can arch away from the migratory surface.
